The clicker questions were a good gauge of your understanding of the lecture, but I would have preferred not paying for it. Clickers were graded based on participation and attendance, but there was a little extra credit for correct answers. There are no curves in this class, and it uses the standard grade cutoffs. Grades are based on the following: 1st midterm (15%), 2nd midterm (20%), final exam (30%), worksheets (22%), online quizzes (10%), and clickers (3%). The weekly online quizzes were based on assigned textbook chapters and were multiple-choice. You had 1 hour to complete them, and they ranged from 10-20 questions. If you read the chapter beforehand (or use ctrl+F), you should have no problem with the time limit and getting 100%. In-class worksheets were completed in randomly-assigned groups of 4, open note, and lasted 1 lecture period. The worksheets were hard, and my group always asked the TAs to help check our answers. The TAs were also very helpful in understanding how to answer the questions. Often, we would be working right up until class ended. They are graded leniently, so as long as your answer is somewhat right, you should get in the A range. The 1st worksheet also had an extra credit question. There were 5 worksheets total, but Dr. Butts said he could change the number for future classes based on student feedback. The answer keys for the worksheets were posted before exams, so we could use them to study. I felt like all the exams were fair and based on the content covered in the class. Dr. Butts said that content covered in the textbook but not covered in lecture could still be on the exams, but he never included them on our exams. The midterms were a mix of multiple choice (around 10 questions) and free response. Some of the multiple-choice questions were taken straight from the online quizzes. The free-response portion included matching, short-answer, long-answer, and drawing graphs. The review questions and worksheets were helpful for studying for the free-response section, but he didn't post an answer key for the review questions. Instead, they were held like a discussion board where multiple students could comment an answer and correct each other, with Dr. Butts providing feedback. If you wanted definitive answers to the review questions, you had to attend either office hours or the exam review session. The exam review sessions were just big office hours held before each exam, but they were helpful for hearing what questions other students asked to double-check your knowledge. The final was split into a comprehensive portion and the last third of the class content. The questions were the same format as the midterms, but it was longer and had proportionally more free-response questions. I didn't feel pressed for time on any of the exams, but I wouldn't recommend spending too much time on any question since some of the free-response questions were lengthy. I studied for the exams by reviewing the lecture recordings and my notes, completing the review questions, going over the worksheet answer keys and quizzes, and attending the exam review session for last-minute questions. Focus more on understanding concepts and the reasons why something happens rather than just memorizing. This wasn't a class to slack off in, but getting an A was completely doable with some effort.

review_text: I had to get a W due to extenuating circumstances, but I wouldn't recommend people to take her after I stayed with her close to the final date. Here are some of the reasons why: Pros: - She is fast-paced and explains things well. - She is willing to chat with you for a little bit of time before and after class, depending on how late/early you have her Cons: - She doesn't really answer students' questions because she's trying to speed through the lecture - She doesn't give you any lecture notes even if you have a university excuse - She only has exam grades in - She gives out some practice problems, but they either are already filled so you can't really practice with them, or they don't have an answer key, so you have to meet or ask in person. Even then, you can't really catch her in person at times because she isn't as flexible with her office hours, so you have to rush to try and get to her before the crowd does. - Even though she gives you past practice exams and other worksheets, she doesn't give you a straightforward way to study for the material that you need for the upcoming exam. She does give you a list of things to "study," but it's a vague list at times, or it has things that weren't discussed in depth. - She moves on from steps and mechanisms that would be good to show, but just tells the class to "do 2 iterations of proton transfer" and doesn't show it Overall: She tends to be really passive-aggressive, which makes you feel like you're not as smart. She isn't really approachable, and she'll make you feel like you aren't smart enough for the class and it's very discouraging for people that are trying and putting in the effort. It's also rough that the TA who teaches isn't as great, since he would gloss over or tell us to "do the work" or call on you when you didn't fully learn the subject or need help with it. The GSS is helpful, but it's nothing like the exam for stocker since she is so synthesis-heavy. I did the practice and exam questions she provides but they're nothing like the actual exam as it's much harder. If you are studying last minute and not putting time into this class thinking you can do the practice exam and be good then you're taking a big risk. There are conceptual questions on the exams that you'll only really know if you study the notes and pay attention to things he emphasizes in lecture. review_text: Oh boy Spring 2025 BSCI223... going to talk about the course first: This class had the highest volume of work I have had in a class here yet. The PAKs are a bit tedious, but they are at least somewhat connected to course material. I really did not like the structure of the class but maybe I just don't get along with flipped classroom. There were a few hours of lecture videos to watch each week, 2 hours of "lecture" (going to the lecture hall to listen to Buchner talk about measles and answer clicker questions), plus 4 hours of lab, plus all of the assignments. BSCI223 is definitely a time suck no matter who the professor is. Lab was honestly pretty fun and we usually got out early. My lab group was chill and we had a good system for getting group assignments done on time. Shoutout my TA Anna, the legend! She was so kind and helpful and always answered everyone's questions. She also held long exam reviews on zoom. Now about Buchner... He isn't as bad as people are saying. I think the comments on his mental state are unfair. Microbiology IS related to the measles outbreak, because types of vaccines are a component of a lecture video and are on the syllabus. It's hard to talk about scientific research in microbiology without mentioning the current state of affairs in scientific research. You really cannot fault Buchner for providing current context. However, I will acknowledge that it took up more time of lecture than it really should have (i.e. mentioning it every day). Exams felt uneven. First one was hard and average was a 66. He gave zero prep materials for it, did not even say what topics would be on it. It included lab stuff which threw everyone off. I know we are in college and we don't need study guides anymore, but it caught everyone off guard. Second exam was better. The final though also had an average of 66. He said it would be cumulative but it really was not. No curve for the class. Essentially: exam 1 = biochem, exam 2 = genetics, exam 3 = immunology. Hopefully you've taken some of those classes and it might help. His "lectures" were sometimes related to the videos, sometimes not. Some were PAK reviews which I found a bit useless. I think this course would work MUCH better if he lectured during lecture, and we answered the clicker questions in a post lecture canvas quiz format. It feels a bit ridiculous to go to 2 hours of lecture just to sit there and do clickers. A moment that is burned into my memory is Buchner flipping out (literally screaming and menacingly walking towards) about an admitted student who came into the lecture hall and took a picture. He started screaming and going off about his intellectual property and how it was against copyright to take pictures of his lecture material. Miss girl I promise you no one wants pictures of your crappy clicker slides.

review_text: TLDR: Dixon's take on this course was pretty unorganized, which had positive (moving back dates of HW deadlines or exams if the majority of the class agreed, index card was allowed, & units were swapped around to match lab) and negative effects (typos, miscommunication, grading errors, lack of current study resources/old exams, & long HWs that feel extra compared to exam content). Sometimes attendance was taken, but other times it wasn't. Exam questions aren't necessarily tricky. They're just long. Some extra credit opportunities through HW & random email tasks. For example, our Exam #1 was pushed back a class, and several HWs were also pushed back. Lecture content aligned well with the lab content, but that doesn't really matter because the lab has a lecture component. She goes over the question types and point breakdowns on the exam before the exam. An index card was allowed for the exams this semester. She seemed indecisive about whether she would keep them for future semesters. Cons: Lots of typos/mistakes in HW & sometimes exams. She often waits very long to announce them. Unclear about the purpose of the required asynchronous lectures. We had several, but only ended up getting tested on one or two topics from them. Crowded office hours. (This may just be a chemistry department problem because I think most of my other professors also had crowded OH) HWs are very difficult and feel too time-consuming for a 2-credit course. They seem to push beyond the understanding needed for the exams, which, according to the TAs, causes people to overthink the exams and fail. CANs aren't technically mandatory, but are essential to understanding HWs. Talks and takes notes kinda fast. No answer keys for old exams. No asynchronous worksheets with problems similar to exams. The CAN worksheets are more similar to HWs and are often used by her to clarify topics she didn't cover well in class that students kept asking about. Notes feel lacking in content. She's mildly straightforward and blunt. I can't speak too much about her personality besides a few email interactions I had with her, and I don't believe spreading other people's interactions I heard about would be the most accurate. Her clarifications in office hours are mildly confusing. She prohibits TAs from helping students with the HW, encouraging them to come to OH and work with others. She grades all the midterms herself. Surprisingly, she's pretty quick with it (Less than 1 week turnaround). My issue is whether she'll get fatigued and start grading differently for people despite similar mistakes, or make grading mistakes. I think the regrading process has been through asking her during office hours, which could lead others to hear the conversation. HW grading between TAs and the final score is very different. Write down the equations as he is teaching, or start the homework before he finishes the chapter, and quizzes will be simple. Homework is 21%, with 14% being masteringphysics and 7% being written. The written is just to do 3 of the masteringphysics problems by hand on paper and turn it in, so it's not really extra work. The masteringphysics tends to be pretty easy, so the homework isn't a huge burden. Do check often if there is an assignment though because he does not announce when he posts them. Do not copy from the solutions manual because they are watching for that and a large portion of the class did just that on the first homework. The exams were each 3 problems and were usually pretty simple. The only issue is that since they are only 3 problems, if you are completely lost on one question, you already lost a large portion of your grade. Study hard for these, redo the masteringphysics, and you'll be fine. The final exam was a common final across all the sections, and was actually pretty easy. review_text: Lab coordinators are usually barely involved with the actual lab, so I can't really fault Koppel for that. However, she still made this lab far more difficult than it needs to be. She's essentially the only person who teaches CHEM232, so there isn't really a chance of avoiding her, it's more about knowing how to approach her lab. The number one thing is that her post-lab questions are ridiculously difficult. These are the questions that she will post on ELMS in addition to the post-lab questions that are already in the lab manual. They will ask hard questions that barely relate to the content of the lab and ask about content that most students don't learn in lecture. Usually, it's not hard to get full points on every other part of the experiments. Those are always graded by your TA (so it's pretty nice to have a chill TA in the class). A lot of times, the pre-lab component is only graded on completion. The post-lab questions (PLQs) are graded on rotation, so they're graded by different TAs every time. Every TA grades a little bit different, and they all grade at different paces, so do not expect to receive your labs back periodically/be able to use your graded labs to help with the future ones. If you want to ensure that you do well on the PLQs, GO TO OFFICE HOURS. Or find a friend who does. A lot of the questions are near impossible to answer unless the TAs tell you the answer. Also, the TAs for my class (Fall 2021) had the answer keys for each lab, so the literal answers were given out at office hours. Koppel eventually realized this and stopped giving them the answer keys, and so the TAs stopped being as helpful, but they were still better than nothing. I always saved doing my lab stuff until the night before, which I really regret. This lab has SO much more work than a one-credit course should have, and it's a good idea to get started on that stuff early so you have time to go to office hours. Also, try and find a TA you like or that other students like, they're likely to be more helpful. I never personally found the pre-lab videos that helpful, but definitely try to watch them, especially for the more complicated labs. Just read the manual closely for each lab and know the directions, it'll make everything go a lot faster (you're gonna wanna get out of those labs as fast as possible, some of them WILL take the full three hours). Besides the lab, there are a few additional assignments, which aren't hard. The midterm in this lab is excessively difficult. There is simply no way to study for it. Koppel published a review guide and it didn't help in any single way. As for the final, Koppel, hosted a review session for the exam, and it was so, so helpful. If she does that again, GO TO IT!! The final felt a lot easier than the midterm for me, and it also wasn't cumulative (just on the second half of the experiments in the course). In a way, there isn't a way to control your grade in this lab. It's impossible to answer questions exactly how Koppel expects. You just have to get through it, unfortunately, there isn't really a way to avoid Koppel.

review_text: The experience you will have on this course is dependent on your lab TA and how cool they are. Mine was super chill and honestly made the class feel not that stressful. The lab manual is written pretty decently and you can ask your TA for clarification if you get confused. Completing the experiment successfully is honestly not that big of a deal as you can just grab someone else's data. They are all honestly pretty easy, but Experiment 5 (Solubility) expects you to place hot test tubes into an ice bath without the glass exploding (some exploded). Lab reports take up a lot of time, but I would recommend doing as much of the post lab questions as you can before you even do the experiment if you have free time during the week. A lot of the questions don't even require the data and are just conceptual questions based on the experiment. It saves you time and also makes what you are doing in the lab make sense. The grading on the lab reports is fair and I only got something other than 95+% on 1 report out of 11. Sometimes lab reports get graded as 0 in canvas before the TA grades them, so you will be stuck with a low grade until the TA grades it. Before every lab you have to do a pre-lab quiz which locks after you take it, so you don't even know the grade you will get or what questions you got wrong until weeks after. They are pretty easy though. You also take post-lab quizzes which are sometimes vague and downright confusing. Expect to get 30-50% on at least 2 of them. I actually saw Dr. Guest because my TA slept in and missed our section. She was actually helpful and was understanding of our situation, and let us off with doing the lab through the lab videos. She also gave our section an extra 3 day extension to turn in the lab report which is why I'm giving her +1 star. What was confusing is what you learn in the lab is ahead of what you learn in CHEM131 lecture, so sometimes you learn concepts in lab first before lecture. Additionally, you have no idea what your final grade is until the end of the semester, and the curve is very weird. I don't know how helpful office hours are because I didn't go to them. Overall, its criminal that this class is only 1 credit and you will spend a lot of time on this class, but if you put in the effort you should get out with a pretty good grade.

review_text: Like many of the people who are probably taking this class, I took it because I'm a biology major who didn't take the AP Bio exam in high school and need to now take the BSCI160-170 sequence. My only gripes with his lectures is that they are very dense and the slides often do not include all of the material. As a result, it was very important to attend class to fill in the gaps with my own notes. His class is definitely not one (as least for me) where you can vaguely listen in to what he was talking about and be able to understand the content well enough for the exams. That's what I did for the first exam and I got an 80.5. To be fair, I lowkey forgot how to study and just looked over the slides as my only method of studying. Once I started actively taking notes (I mean like literally writing down everything he said during class) I got 91 and 98 on midterms two and three and a 91 on the final. The content itself is not difficult, but you need to know EVERYTHING on the slides because it's all fair game. The examples mentioned in class (accompanied with diagrams) may only seem like examples, but you WILL be tested on them on the midterms, so if you don't know the specificities of a table or graph you might lose easy points. Personally, I found that making thorough flashcards after each lecture was the best way to study. Make sure that you include in your flashcards all the details in both the slides and the visuals on the slides (there are some definitions on the visuals as well that you might not notice). I went over the flashcards a couple days before the exams and was able to score well on midterms 2 & 3. Overall, I'd say the exams were very fair. Everything tested is from the slides. You will not need the textbook at all, so don't bother buying it. The homeworks were tedious at times, but they definitely helped with the overall understanding of the content. Lots of the exam questions end up being exact copies of the questions on the homework. What's really nice is that the lowest midterm is dropped and you get to bring an index card (front and back) to the midterms. For the final you get a full sheet of paper (only the front). Overall, I would take this class again. Dr. Shapiro is so incredibly passionate about the subject. The last couple of classes where he discusses human impact on the environment were especially interesting even though they were a bit doom and gloom. Coming from someone who isn't too passionate about ecology and evolution, Dr. Shapiro has definitely ignited some passion in the subject matter for me.

review_text: For those considering taking the class because of the high grade distribution, DO NOT BE FOOLED. I spoke with MULTIPLE TAs at both the undergraduate and graduate levels. Now that all exams are closed-book and in-person, the average grade is now in the B+ range. IT IS NOT EASY to get an A without stressing out of your mind. Now for my review: This class was genuinely not worth the amount of effort I put in and the stress it caused. I am a chemistry major, Pre-med (thus took this class), and this was the MOST time-consuming thing I had this entire semester. Not even research or Orgo 2 took this much energy out of me. The "flipped classroom" layout leads to people not watching lecture videos for months on end, and the lab work doesn't even help you learn the concepts that well most of the time. The lab is basically just "can you read instructions" and "can you analyze research articles about random microbiology topics." The exams are also something I have a bone to pick with, because there was absolutely no practice for any of the exams. Granted, however, if you keep up with the videos and lecture stuff, you will probably do pretty well on the exams, and the exams are the most grade-determining assignments. The first exam was super free, but subsequent exams just got worse and worse. The second exam had an average so bad Dr. Tran had to curve by giving everyone 10 points (dub for me, but if you had C on the exam, it didn't do much for you). The final, which I just took today, was literally just the hardest parts of every single midterm plastered into one exam and you had to relate it to the new material. NO CONSISTENCY AT ALL. I wouldn't even be mad if the exams were slightly harder, but at least make them all similar so we know what to expect man. ALL IN ALL: Worst part of this class is the busy work. I maintained a 97 in organic chem 2 with no problem but this class's formatting and work is somehow 4x worse on my mental. Exams basically determine your grade, but they aren't the worst part by far. Take this class only if you need to, or if you really really like microbio and don't want to take the upper-level class for it. The A wasn't even that free, and it was way too much stress for this stupid class. The prof isnt bad, this overall is just a review of the terrible class layout, format, and assignments.

review_text: Let me start off by saying that Professor Fernandes is a very nice guy. He treats students with respect, and he's always willing to answer any questions that students have during the lectures. But I would also say that if you value your sanity, or you have a super duper packed schedule as is, do not take Professor Fernandes. You are better of taking the same class with a different professor. For starters, during the lectures, a lot of what he teaches is the theoretical stuff, with regards to how to derive different formulas that are already in the notes packets that he gives. Some of them are not in the notes packets, though, and you will only learn it if you actually attend his lecture and take notes. So you never want to miss any of his classes if you do end up taking his class. That's fine and all. My biggest gripe with this course is with regards to how he organizes them. He gives quizzes every week, but really no material to help you practice for those quizzes ahead of time. He kind of just expects you to understand what he teaches in the lectures and use just that to prepare for the quizzes. The problem is that his lectures are theoretical, and his quizzes are very application based. Without any practice problems to prepare for the quizzes ahead of time, it becomes very easy for the quizzes to throw you off. One time, these two students asked him if he can give some practice problems before the quiz to help them better prepare for it. He then went on a tangent about how you should be taking notes, and if you don't understand something, ask your fellow classmate. He claimed that he is teaching for the "average student," but the truth is that the average student would appreciate better organization and more practice. He asked those two students if it would really be worth their time to do 15 questions before the quiz, as if that would be a bad thing. But the truth is, yes, spending extra time on practice problems for this course would be so worth it. And trust me, using ChatGPT to prepare for the quizzes won't help. No LLM will cover the nuances of the questions that Professor Fernandes likes to ask. Hell, even if he doesn't give practice problems, you would hope that he gives you homework problems before the quizzes to work through. Nope. Most of the time, he gives the homeworks only after the quizzes. The homeworks are definitely useful to prepare for the exams, though. His exams are very, very fair. I have no gripes about that. Just be careful with some nuances of the problems, and you'll be destined for success on the exams. One thing that I want to note is that for homeworks, make sure that there are no mistakes before you submit them. Partial credit is sometimes not a concept when your homework is being graded. Because of that, you could make a small mistakes and you will lose full points for the question. Same thing goes for quizzes. These are graded by TAs, not Professor Fernandes. The exams are graded by Professor Fernandes, and he grades them very fairly. Overall, I think Professor Fernandes is a nice guy, but I really do think that he is failing to understand his students and what exactly would help them succeed better in his class. He also doesn't do a super great job of mitigating any uncertainty in the class, and that can be quite stressful when you already have quite a packed and difficult schedule. Because of this, I would say that it's better worth your time to take this class with a different professor, because they give you more resources and teach more of the application stuff, which is what is necessary for exams and quizzes in the first place.

review_text: Fawzi is my favorite professor I’ve ever had so far at UMD, at least as it stands through my first year. His exams consistently have pretty high scores, take mostly lighter content from the lecture, and are basically what you expect from going to lecture. review_text: I didn't take PHYS131, so I was a little worried about how I would do in this class, but it was surprisingly simple. The lectures have all of the information you need to take the exams and complete the homework, so I didn't need to review any 131 topics that might not be covered in a conventional physics class. Dr. Severson was a good lecturer; he spoke slowly and clearly and sometimes drew diagrams to assist his explanations. I think he gives a little too much time to answer clicker questions, but they're nice as a brain break, and he explains the answers afterward. He's not the most passionate teacher and tends to read off the slides, but most of the class is just here for the credit anyway. He records his lectures. Attendance is not mandatory, and the in-lecture clicker questions can be completed outside of lecture. Doing the lab reports was a bit of a challenge since I wasn't used to their format, but I had good teammates who knew what they were doing, and I learned through observation. If you took PHYS131, the lab reports are in the same tedious format. Make sure you pay attention to the rubrics for the lab reports and try to do the modeling section in lab so you can ask the TA questions. The last couple of lab reports were easier than the first ones since they had you answer specific questions instead of a conventional report. All the lab reports were completed in groups, so make sure you pick good teammates. The lab scores get normalized at the end of the semester, so some people ended up with over 100% for their lab grade. There is a recitation you're supposed to complete each lab that's graded for participation, but some TAs don't really care if you do them. Lab content has no bearing on the exams. Other than lab reports, the only other assignments we have are the Expert TA homework and the TopHat clicker questions, both of which you have to pay for. The clicker questions (both in-lecture and for homework) are generally graded for completion. Sometimes there are TopHat quizzes in lecture graded for accuracy, but Dr. Severson warns you about them ahead of time, and they're not difficult. You can also talk to your classmates to verify answers. The Expert TA questions are graded for accuracy, so I'd recommend completing them on a sheet of paper, verifying your answers with a TA, then submitting them online. There are 10 graded Expert TA assignments, and some are longer than others, so make sure to check them before deciding to do them last minute. There are 3 exams total (2 midterms and a final), with the final worth 17% of your grade and each midterm worth 14%. All the content you need to know is covered in the lecture, so I didn't really use the textbook to study. So if you're a senior looking for an easy, low-effort class take 421 with Reggia, but if you actually want to learn something I suggest you look elsewhere.

review_text: Chacko's grading scheme is pretty fair. If you attain maximum points on the homework (14 assignments worth 2 points each, maximum points to earn is 20), get the one homework question completely correct on the midterm, and both homework questions completely correct on the final, then you get a C. He makes it clear from the get-go that getting an A is not an easy task. That said, if you work hard on the homework, it'll probably carry over the midterm. I felt like I did terribly on the midterm, maybe getting a C but bracing for worse, but I ended up getting an A. He engages the students in questioning during lecture to keep them active in coming up with physical reasoning or making observations about physical systems that lead to the course content he wants to deliver. His examples, while right out of the book, were still very helpful and usually presented with much more clarity than in the text. I think I learned more in this class than any other physics class I've had up to this point (and there are still things I should go back to review!). (And don't get me wrong - while I worked hard and think I should go back and study even more, I'm not an exemplary student. When Chacko said we should be working extra problems from the text, even should be reading the text, and said we should be reading extra textbooks, I was mildly terrified that that was what was expected of me if I was to ever succeed in physics. I mean, when do I get the time to do all this stuff? I think if you have good attention to the physics of classical systems, and good intuition about how systems should behave, then you'll do fine.)

review_text: Dr. Truman is awesome. I've honestly had a blast, and that's largely due to how she runs the course. I don't think I'm particularly smart (or math-y), but I've found she makes the content not only accessible, but exciting as well (looking to future semesters). In particular, some of the stuff I find super helpful: - focuses on building intuition for what we're doing, and is happy to slow down and/or reexplain as needed. for more challenging chapters, we'd take it even slower than usual (1 week+ per chapter). - building off the last point, she really values understanding over semantics/the minutiae. The review below mine is correct that she doesn't curve, but that's because there's a curve built into the class! The majority of the points earned outside of quizzes/exams are completion-based, and even on the quizzes and exams the grading again mostly (~70%) focuses on understanding (rather than punishing algebra mistakes or a skipped minor step). this is something she actually emphasizes throughout the course, eg encouraging people to at least write a solid outline of the given proof and define variables to get partial credit if nothing else/the approach isn't jumping out. - the more or less weekly groupworks/quizzes are fantastic. the problems she's written have been great for both consistently challenging my understanding and reminding me of definitions/theorems/techniques I should probably spend more time on (and during the groupwork, she and her TA walk around the class, interacting/helping groups as needed work through the problems) - office hours are a great resource. she knows the common points of confusion for both course material and the homeworks, and is always happy to give that little (or big) hint to help you continue to progress through it. furthermore, she also has a pretty active Piazza class which she encourages people to post on as needed for homework hints, quiz/exam review, or just clarification. - i said it above but she really is just awesome. she's super personable, willing to negotiate deadlines if you have something pop up, and is just generally excited about the class. i know it's probably the millionth time she's covered the material, and yet she still brings energy and enthusiasm to every single one of her lectures. Another issue wasn't really with him, but with how class was structured (unsure if this is the professor or department's doing). It makes no sense that two midterms are worth 50%, the final is 40%, and then the 11 problem sets, which easily took 30-40 hours total (atleast for me), are only worth 10%. There’s technically extra credit, but it’s just ~1%, which doesn’t change much. I get that AI makes cheating on homework easier, but this grading setup feels like an overcorrection. Some people are naturally better at proof-style exam problems, and the weighting heavily favors them. Without a curve, the averages were borderline failing. The testbank practice finals weren't much help either, as past professors often taught entirely different topics and/or from different texts. I feel like if your brain doesn't think the way the problems want you to, you get punished for it. I'll ask clarification occasionally but I don't want to be raising my hand throughout the class. In other words, some more emphasis on the thought-process step-by-step would be useful is all.

There were only 5 homework assignments, very doable with the TA's available over email for extra help, and never took me much more than an hour. Some took fewer than 30 minutes. I am aware of many people doing them last minute the night before they were due, which I would just never recommend because then there is far less time to receive help if you end up needing it. I'm not sure if people who had bad things to say about Fagan were just not showing up, not paying attention or just taking notes straight from the slides. I can say that there was a noticeable drop in attendance after the first week, and he even showed us in the beginning of the semester grade distributions for those who attended nearly every lecture vs those who did not. Again, even though attendance isn't graded, this is college. Just show up twice a week. I feel as though I didn't have to go above and beyond to do very well in this course. I just showed up, listened and took notes, and used the resources he gave us (and even then sometimes did bare minimum). The TA's were also very helpful, and do deserve a shout out as well. This is not a throwaway class, and if you are in a science major you will likely face so much worse than this very manageable class. review_text: One of the best math professors I've ever had. The course is based on the first 7 chapters of Baby Rudin, and the content is often dense and difficult, but Panos' teaching is excellent. He goes through all the proofs step-by-step and asks questions in a way that is engaging and makes it interactive so we learn the content better. His responses to students' questions are also very helpful. The course grade is 10% homework, 30% for each of the two midterms, and 30% for the final. The problems for most of the homework assignments and exams were exercises from the textbook, which were often very difficult (with exams taking 3-6 hours). However, this was balanced by the fact that the they were all take-home, and we had 24 hours for each of them. Homework was graded on completion. After talking to friends who took 410 with another professor, I feel that I took away much more from this class by taking it with Panos. As a postdoc, he truly cares about his students and wants them to learn and appreciate math instead of having to worry about grades or assignments. He is clearly passionate about the subject and often connects the proofs we write in class to how mathematicians work, giving us a glimpse of what doing real math looks like. I came away from the course with a solid understanding of basic topology, sequences and series, differentiation, etc. The only reason I am taking off one star is that I feel the homework and exams would benefit from having more easy-medium and fewer hard problems. I think that this would help me with practicing my understanding of the course concepts and gauging my understanding of where I'm at with the material.

review_text: This was my favorite class this semester. I really liked lectures, he was very approachable in office hours, homeworks were sufficiently challenging without feeling overboard most of the time, the content was interesting to me. I don't know, this class just did it for me. I talked to some people about taking this class and not having taken MATH403 yet, and a few have questioned me for doing so. While basic content from that class may be helpful for this class, MATH403 is in no way an implicit prerequisite for this professor's MATH405 (it may be for some sections, though I don't know personally). Positivity is hard to write about, so I'll put a few things I didn't quite like about this class here. For one, homeworks are physically handed in during class. I do all my work digitally, and printers are my worst nightmare, so this bugged me quite a bit, even though I attended every class anyways. Exams are heavily weighted, as each midterm is 25%, and the final is 40%, with the remaining 10% being homeworks. This isn't quite as bad as it could be, as the exams were rather easy all things considered, and each of them come with a bit of extra credit, but it's something to keep in mind if exams aren't your strongsuit. The textbook we used, Linear Algebra Second Edition by Hoffman and Kunze, isn't bad by any means, but I didn't like some aspects of it. There are some problems in the book which aren't the most clear due to having wonky English, using terminology which hasn't been fully established (independent set comes to mind, where the book means linearly independent set without first establishing that fact, where independent set is a term from graph theory), or having odd symbol usage (using \to instead of \mapsto for mappings, for example). In general, I generally prefer how Linear Algebra Done Right by Sheldon Axler presents information, and used it as a second reference on a few occasions throughout the course. Finally, one particular lecture after exam 2 felt very rushed, which was rather annoying given that a homework on the topic was assigned that day and due the next class (usually, a full week is given to do ahttps://youtu.be/XjZHAa4hR68 homework). For me, my gripes are minor in the grand scheme of things. I highly recommend this professor for MATH405.

review_text: One of the easier upper level CS courses in that the material isn't conceptually demanding (compared to some of the low-level or mathy upper level CS courses). A better title for this course is "Mobile App Development" ("Programming Handheld Systems" can be misleading for embedded systems folks), and Dr. Franceschi uses Kotlin/Android Studio (as opposed to Flutter or React Native). Hence, a big part of doing well in the course is to familiarize yourself with Kotlin syntax and Android Studio, which he provides plenty of resources for. What you learn is relevant to mobile app development in general, regardless of the language/framework that's used in class. Syntax is the first thing you learn when picking up a new language, often followed by learning to read documentation. Writers of some of the other reviews seemed to miss this. If you're reading the other reviews for this course that complain about "unfair/pointless" grading, lack of a cheatsheet, points taken off for incorrect code logic, or other easily solvable concerns – keep in mind that in any course that emphasizes learning a new language or framework, you are tested on your knowledge of the language/framework, NOT how well you can use an IDE or autocomplete. If you're proficient in ANY object-oriented programming language, then you know the learning curve is steepest at the start. Stay up-to-date with the material for the first 1-2 weeks, and you'll quickly learn what approach works best for you with regards to grasping the material As for the class/grading structure, this is how it was for Fall 2025 (you can decide what's a pro or a con): - Dr. Franceschi posted all code and slides from class, and recorded every lecture to watch - in decreasing order of what was weighted most: final exam, total project grade, midterm, group project, quizzes. I understand the annoyance with quizzes because they could consist of questions from a range of given topics, and to do well you're inclined to knowing absolutely everything which makes them exam-like. Nonetheless, Dr. Franceschi doesn't throw curveballs, and the quizzes were the exact same in structure and style as the practice ones he posted. And doing bad on some quizzes won't kill your grade. - homeworks are projects, which were straightforward, and tweaking code examples from class/Canvas will help you a TON. - as with any group assignment: what makes/breaks your grade is your group; at worst, you'll end up doing more work than you intended. As long as the final result follows the rubric, there's nothing to worry about (you won't have to publish your app nor will outsiders be testing it). - midterm/final exams felt very long; exam questions matched practice questions in structure and style. Completing projects is the best way to prepare for the exams, followed by skimming through the code and class examples afterwards. He gave us documentation sheets with some class/functions/interfaces/variables that were on the exam, which guarantees free points if you know how to read. Regrade requests were addressed quickly. - Personal opinions: Dr. Franceschi's lecturing style is monotonous and not the most engaging, but it's far better than a professor who rushes or teaches like everyone already knows everything. He's respectful and clear about the class structure (and any changes to it that come up). Use the recordings to your advantage. I'd rate the course a 4.5/5 if I could. This is a lengthy review, but one that hopefully clears up some misconceptions about the course.

Lectures can be rather dense at times, but the slides are explained clearly during class and broken down into simpler explanations. In terms of the actual content taught in BSCI410, a recurring theme is applicability. Dr. Wu structures the course to cover aspects of biology that students can actually apply to careers in biology and genetics. This includes introducing commonly used techniques and methods as well as experimental designs and analysis. A recent development for the course that I appreciated was the introduction of bioinformatics assignments. As an increasing amount of research relies on RNA sequencing, proteomics, etc, having the skills in R to create graphs and interpret data is vital. I would argue that this class has more assignments (homework, short essays, quizzes, etc) than most of my other upper level BSCI classes, but they aid in understanding and give you additional practice. To help students outside of the lecture and office hours, Dr. Wu encourages students to ask questions on the class Piazza. Whether it is for homework, classwork, exams, or just curiosity, TA’s and Dr. Wu provided thorough replies in a timely manner. Overall, I would highly recommend taking BSCI410 with Dr. Wu. review_text: First, I'm just going to start by saying, for CMSC330, it really doesn't matter much who your professor is. The lecture quizzes, projects, discussion content, TAs, quizzes, and exam content are all exactly the same. The only difference between Cliff and Anwar's sections are which professor's lecture you can attend, but even then, you can just not go to lecture or go to the other professor's lecture (some people found that they didn't really like Cliff's lectures and attended Anwar's instead---the class is big enough that I don't think people would notice). Unlike CMSC351, the professor doesn't make that much of a difference for this class, so don't freak out too much. That being said, I do think Dr. Mamat has the better slides and also more experience in the field, so if you do have a choice, I would probably choose him. Here are my comments on the course in general (this applies for both Dr. Mamat and Cliff's sections): - All the class information is available here: https://bakalian.cs.umd.edu/330 - Literally 44% of your grade is free. Why do I say this? Projects make up 40% of your grade and you get around two weeks for each of them (give or take). You can ask questions, ask the TAs, look up documentation, submit as many times as you want, etc. within those two weeks. Each project took me between two and eight hours. There is literally no reason not to get 100% on every project as long as you don't procrastinate. The median on every project was between 97% to 100%. So again, there's literally no reason not to get 100% on every project, and they make up 40% of your grade. - 4% of your grade is lecture quizzes, which are completely open internet. You can run the code on your own machine, and the lowest couple of lecture quizzes get dropped. So between the lecture quizzes and the projects, 44% of your grade should be completely free (as long as you don't procrastinate). - The quiz medians were: Quiz 1: 14.5/20, Quiz 2: 15/20, Quiz 3: 17.25/20, Quiz 4: 16/20. You get access to all of the course's quizzes and solutions from previous semesters, which is helpful for studying. I honestly found the quizzes to be harder than the midterms. I will say, though, that I didn't do very well on the first two quizzes, but after that, I started buckling down and really studying and I got 100s on the last two quizzes. You'll be fine as long as you study and really understand the content. - 46% of your grade is two midterms and the final. The medians were: Midterm 1: 83, Midterm 2: 87.5, Final (with extra credit): 89.48. Just like the quizzes, you get access to every previous midterm and their answer key, and around ~85% of the content on these exams is the same every semester. They do change things up a bit sometimes (like I think we did more garbage collection than they did in previous semesters), but most of the exams cover very similar content to previous semesters, so it's really helpful to take previous exams for practice. And yes, there's extra credit too. - The discussions were fine. I didn't find them too helpful. There were good review questions, but they were all in a publicly-available GitHub repository that you could look at without going to discussion. Honestly, unless you're really confused about something, you can usually just look up your question online or on Piazza. There are a gazillion resources out there for Ocaml and Rust. For Cliff in particular, I thought his lectures are okay. He goes at a very manageable pace; definitely not fast by any means. He can get pretty theoretical sometimes. He answers questions well. TLDR; This is a fairly easy class as long as you don't procrastinate on your projects and do previous quizzes/exams as practice. I would recommend not starting the projects any later than the weekend before they're due. You could definitely knock them out over the weekend (if you don't mind working on the weekends). I thought the content was fairly interesting, although obviously that's extremely subjective and is up to how interested you are in this type of stuff. I would recommend taking Dr. Mamat but it really doesn't matter that much.

review_text: As a 1 credit course, like the other reviews say, this class is a LOT of work and very disorganized. Oftentimes you will find yourself writing the same things in many different places. But really, it is not horribly difficult, just rather time consuming. Points go as following: 5 points for the pre-lab quiz (pretty straightforward if you read the procedure), 5 points for the notebook pages (pretty straightforward too), 20 points for the worksheets (straightforward as long as you did the experiment or the makeup), and 20 points for either the PLQ (post lab questions) or TAQ (theory and applications quiz)...and no, they are not as notorious as people say. All you need to do for PLQs to do well on them (coming from someone who repeatedly scored 90%+ on them) is to understand the procedure of the lab: not necessarily which chemicals were used, but the objective of the lab. Essentially, they are to apply the objective of the lab to a different set of chemicals, as a sort of "what if" situation. Office hours help A LOT. Sometimes they were very confusing, other times pretty easy. But do not ever wait last minute to do them, that's how you screw up. TAQs are like PLQs, but instead of having a week or two to do it, you have only 10 minutes in class. These...are horrible to say the least. Because they are so rushed, getting a 10/20 or above will feel like luck. Class averages for these being under 5/20 are no exaggeration. Overall, it is possible to do well in the course. You just need to be able to understand the objective of each procedure to pass.

review_text: This is a review after taking the course in Summer 2026 (June 2 to July 25). It's an 8-week course assigning about 1 to 2 hours of content per day (excluding weekends, holidays, and days before exams). Content mainly consists of videos, with occasional interactive Python notebooks and PDFs of lecture notes. The videos are pre-recorded sessions of Teli switching between PowerPoint slides and an overhead view of him writing on paper. They walk through the math behind foundational machine learning algorithms, like computing entropy and information gain for decision trees or tracing partial derivatives for backpropagation. Grading breakdown: 25% homework, 25% projects, 25% midterm, 25% final. Homeworks are ELMS Canvas quizzes with no time limit, usually allowing 2 to 3 attempts. Answers unlock after the final submission. Projects involve working with notebooks to implement core logic behind classifiers, regressors, and neural nets, essentially building a basic Scikit-learn-like backend. The setup expects you to test code by running python.exe commands through a Conda environment, which can feel clunky compared to using a modern IDE. Some code may also need fixing due to outdated syntax or dependencies. It's generally easy to get 100% on all projects and homework, plus some optional extra credit on Project 3 that can add up to 1.25% to your final grade. As others have noted, most of the weight falls on the midterm and final. About half the practice exam content matched what appeared on the actual tests. The rest depends on your study coverage. Some 20- to 30-point questions may catch you off guard if you haven’t reviewed all concepts, algorithm traces, math derivations, or the optional textbook (ciml-v0_9-all). Overall, the course is structured and well-paced for 8 weeks. While some topics or variations are trimmed or glossed over due to time constraints, which the professor openly acknowledges, it’s clear he enjoys the material and puts in consistent effort to explain each concept in a way that builds understanding for the viewer.

review_text: I've never seen a professor where the reviews capture the experience so accurately, but this one really does. The most important thing to know about this class, imo, is that it is HARD. The hardest CS class I've ever taken by far, and I took 351 with Kruskal; Kruskal's 351 is a cake walk compared to this class. However the difference is that you learn SO MUCH and just about EVERYTHING is useful and applicable to the real world. I went into this class knowing next to nothing about networks, but now I can tell you just about everything that happens to get information from one device to another. All the big fun networks words and acronyms like IP, TCP, UDP, HTTP, Wi-Fi, Ethernet, DNS, etc... you learn it all and you learn it WELL. Want to know how an email is actually sent or how the Dark Web works? Take this class. You will learn more in this class than like, three semesters full of other classes. It's ridiculous and awesome. His policy is "there is no magic", and his goal is to teach you to understand all of the "magic" that happens to make the Internet exist. And I feel like he accomplished that. Bobby really is an abrasive professor and can be quite rude to students, but I genuinely think he means no harm, he's just trying to make people laugh. And man, he really is funny. One of the funnier professors I've had. In the same vein, the dude is super charismatic and class is just generally enjoyable with him once you realize that his "rudeness" is really mostly good natured. He also responds to Piazza posts in mere minutes, and genuinely seems like he wants you to succeed. But also, the projects were really, really hard. I especially didn't like that we were just expected to learn socket programming from scratch and just do it for the first couple projects, before learning what sockets even were. We eventually did learn the protocols and such that make sockets work about a third of the way into the class, but the projects expected that well before then. And they only got harder, and I got some grades on the projects in the 10-30% range even after a whole lot of work. You do have to sacrifice a LOT of time to these projects, and it is really hard to do so. This is why the class is so hard. Some of them are extremely cool though once they work. And yeah, the exams were hard, but fair, but long. Time crunch for sure. I would seriously recommend taking this class but taking ZERO other hard classes alongside it, because you need an egregious amount of time to do well in this class. I don't even know if I'm going to pass but it was seriously worth it anyway because of how much cool, useful, and important stuff I learned about how things in the real world work.

review_text: Not bad for a first time! This class consisted of 3 exams and homework, weighted 60% and 40% respectively. Homework was graded mostly for completion (the grader usually graded only one question, and averages were around 95% for each). Exams were pretty difficult, though she adjusted for this as the class went on, as she didn't expect the first test to have a low average (62% iirc). She expects extremely well-written proofs, so especially if you came from a more lenient background, it can be quite jarring to lose points in places you don't expect. There is a small-ish curve at the end of the class (1.5% if I had to guess), and she also held two re-exams for the class, one to replace the first test grade, the second on a new topic to increase by the average of the lowest exam and retake (it was weird). Zomback is a pretty great lecturer, and she's always quite clear and willing to answer questions. Most of the concepts are technically rehashes of Calc 1 in a proof-based setting, so it's not usually that new, but she helps make things easier to parse through. She's also extremely helpful in office hours, and has always been able to answer the questions I had regarding Homework and Tests! The only two main gripes I would have with this class are the difficulty in really understanding how to write proofs perfectly and the re-exams in general. Because the homework is graded leniently, ironically enough, it makes the exams a bit harder (in my opinion), as you can't tell how to write proofs. Some people can probably write proofs well the first time, but it was quite difficult to freestyle, even if that's kind of part of the class. Also, I personally didn't like the re-exams (compared to a curve). This is mostly preference, but I could not do well on any re-exams for the life of me :/. They did increase the average, though, leading to medians of both exams being mid-80s. Overall, though, Professor Zomback is a great teacher!

review_text: I agree that the other reviews have been too harsh. My impression of the class is that the workload is high, but you will learn a lot. I felt that the grading was lenient despite the high workload. The majority of the workload comes from the reading homeworks before each class. They are advertised to be 1.5 hours, but I regularly spent more than that on them. They are also not easy, and you can’t expect to get all the questions right. The clicker questions are similar to the reading homeworks, but they are more lenient since multiple answers can be correct. Unfortunately, I noticed that after doing the reading homeworks, the lectures were a bit stale since they mostly rehashed the content covered in the homeworks. The 4 projects have one of the most lenient late penalties I’ve ever seen, with 2.5% off per day late. Overall they were not too bad, comparable to the workload of CMSC420 projects. The last 2 projects were different since they used an established codebase. I spent a lot of time on those projects jumping around the codebase and trying to figure out what was going on. The exams were challenging and similar to the reading homeworks and clicker questions. The final exam was surprising compared to other finals in that there were almost no “gimmes” that I could answer quickly and move on. Instead of asking “do you remember this definition/formula/question”, most of them looked like “can you use the underlying concept and apply it to new situations”. For me the HW and clicker questions, along with the practice exams, were the best way to prepare. Because of that, I think you gotta lock in the entire semester, more so than other courses, to be able to digest and understand the questions at a reasonable pace. I don’t think cramming by reading through the slides and memorizing formulas would be very successful for these exams. Overall, I’d say this is one of the harder CS electives out there. The ceiling for workload is high in that there’s a lot of content and you can end up spending a lot of time on it. Even without reaching that ceiling, I think it’s possible to get a good grade with the curves.

review_text: I think Fawzi is a pretty reasonable professor. Firstly, he's (generally) a great lecturer which I appreciate more than I can convey considering I am someone who usually goes to her classes. Exam #2, he told us to review definitions. What do you know? We're asked to write out a theorem on the exam. The people who weren't in lecture were cooked. You probably will be too because Fawzi clearly puts a lot of emphasis on going to lecture. 2) Pay attention in lecture. I try to take notes while he's talking but do whatever works for you. This will make step #3 significantly easier. 3) If he does a problem in lecture, do it again, by yourself, at home. This is a 4 credit (I think) college-level math course. You're not going to learn everything just by sitting in lecture. If anything isn't absolutely crystal clear to you (and even if you think it is), do it again. This really isn't half as hard as it sounds as long as you do it immediately after lecture instead of allowing the lectures to pile up. review_text: Amazing professor. Getting a lot of dislike now from people who were expecting A's with not a lot of work. The exams are difficult, of course, but it's organic chemistry. You can't dislike a professor because she didn't give you an easy A in a difficult course. What sets Dr. Hirschauer apart is she helps you to succeed. To any future students: any of the people telling you that you'd be better off taking other professors like stocker/koppel aren't being realistic. Those professors would have been just as difficult if you don't put in work. She has very reasonable expectations, honestly much more lenient, compared to other professors as well. She does not emphasize unnecessary memorization for things like super specific pKa values or complicated mechanisms or nomenclature. She makes the course manageable. Things about the class I liked: Hirschauer provides a practice problem set ranging from easy to difficult for every single chapter we go through as well as talked-through explanations. These are SO helpful, make sure to do them. Some of the more difficult problems definitely reflect what's on the exam. Make sure you're able to actually understand what you're doing for all of them. She gives you a homework category worth 10% with 8 attempts each, basically allowing you to continue to try until you have a full understanding of the content. It's meant to help you learn, not reduce your grade, and you can go to her and ask her for help on anything you genuinely don't understand, so make sure to try the homework in advance. Another bonus: these are on Canvas and she doesn't require you to go buy or use some alternate (and often hard to use) homework platform. Her lecture guides are the best. You can follow along with what she's teaching without having to rush to write every tiny detail on your own—I wish I had this for other classes too. With more difficult areas of ochem, she provides past lecture videos so you can hear things a second time. Her lecture notes are also scanned and uploaded. She genuinely has so many resources for you to succeed, just make sure you are taking advantage of them and go back to your notes if you have a question/approach her! She has a charismatic personality that makes lecture fun and even entertaining at times. Without her teaching, I would've enjoyed this subject a lot less. You can also tell that she loves to teach, which is something that is reflected in how many resources she has for us to succeed. Addressing other comments: 1) she does spend time in lecture making sure people's questions are answered, and many times people's questions will be on very basic concepts. That does not mean that she is trying to spend time answering basic concepts, just that she's responding to questions. 2) As for the curve, it was honestly pretty generous. Based on exam performance, since final exam cutoffs aren't released (as is standard for chemistry), low 80s are usually an A or A-. 3) The lecture examples often reflected basic ideas because we were learning them for the first time. Make sure to go over the notes, but don't rely on these as your sole source of studying, there are practice problem sets for a reason. The exam matches the difficulty of the practice problem sets too. Additional comments: GSS leaders were so helpful. The ones this semester, Alice and Aubrey, were great. Make sure you try going, and even if you don't, the worksheets are provided to try (and you should do them for extra practice!!). But still, try going in person because they explain things so well. Also, study in advance. Try to keep up with content in advance of the exam because the course will go by fast (she tries to keep time for review days). review_text: Course: This is a course on Electromagnetism. Concepts will be harder to understand than those from Physics I because they relate to more abstract concepts, but as long as you spend a good amount of time understanding those concepts the exams shouldn't be a hard time. According to the schedule Hailu is supposed to go up to Chapter 16 in the textbook and even talk about Thermodynamics, but this semester and I think the last semester as well he only got up to Chapter 14. So just keep that in mind. Lecture: Hailu is a pretty slow lecturer and often goes through pretty long derivations and also spends quite a bit of time on practice problems. I found this approach useful to me but if you find yourself relying on the textbook a lot to understand the concepts it might not be the best idea to go to lecture. The only thing is Hailu doesn't post his lecture notes or records (unless class is canceled), and in my opinion his walkthroughs of the lecture problems are really important. So if you plan to not come to lecture try to get a friend who does go to share their notes with you. Discussion: Hailu claims you learn new material in discussion but pretty much all the discussions were just reviewing concepts from lecture. If you are good with what was in the lecture there isn't much reason to go to discussion. My TA in particular seemed to do problems that were way harder than the ones Hailu gave in lecture or in the exams. Main benefit of discussion is you can discuss HW problems with the TA. Homework: Homeworks are pretty easy for the most part as they mostly resemble lecture problems, and a lot of them just involve you deriving formulas (that were already covered in lecture) and then substituting in the values. You get 5 tries with each open-ended problem and no points are taken off until you use up all 5 tries, so use them wisely. Homeworks come every week and are due the next week. The homework is also really good practice for the exams so I'd recommend studying those problems before them. Quizzes: Quizzes are only worth 10% of the grade and there were only 8 of them this semester. One of them was also dropped. These mostly cover conceptual questions, so review the posted slides and lecture problems prior to doing these quizzes. If you get a question wrong your quiz grade can drop quite a bit, but like I said they are only 10% so don't worry too much about not doing good on these. Just make sure you aren't consistently bombing the quizzes by studying the material beforehand. Exams: Each exam consisted of 3 questions (6 for the final) with multiple parts. Hailu likes to have his questions build on each other so you'll want to make sure you understand the relationships between the concepts you learn in class and relationships built across the chapters. Hailu allows you to use an equation sheet. I'd recommend filling that sheet with every equation he covers in lecture, as the exams can consist of any question type. As long as you understand the concepts Hailu's exams aren't really too difficult, as once you figure out the concept and which equation to use the actual question becomes very simple. Other Random Advice - Don't go too crazy studying practice problems. Study the lecture problems and HW problems and if you understand those, you should be good. If you don't understand them, then you may want to try your hand at the extra textbook problems. - Use discussion/office hours to clarify concepts. - Hailu curves the class in the sense that if the class average is below what it should be, he'll make it so 20% get A's, 40% get B's, 25% get C's, the rest get D or F. So as long as you put in a decent effort you shouldn't worry too much about failing this class, even if you aren't so good with physics. Class Review: My 4-star rating is mostly because of how easy the exams are, as they made the class a lot less stressful for me. Otherwise Hailu is mostly an average professor for me. He goes over the material decently well and he goes over many problems in class. The main caveat is he doesn't post solutions or record, which felt unnecessary since I'm sure neither of those things are very hard to do and would have made reviewing the lecture problems a lot less of a hassle. Overall, if you take PHYS260 with Hailu you really shouldn't have too much of a problem. Putting in the effort should be enough to get a decent grade.

Usually, their reasoning was something like, "He's all over the place and is impossible to follow," or, "I feel like we don't learn anything in the class". What that illustrates is that they're not accustomed to rigorous, difficult math courses and that they're either too lazy or not apt enough to study and understand the deeper concepts that are actually worth putting the time and effort in for. One kid in the class said that "Modular arithmetic is dumb because there are no formulas." If you associate yourself with people like that then I recommend dropping out of any upper-level math courses and taking something more your style like communications. In summation, I highly recommend Dr. Ramachandran to anyone who is a serious and mature student and/or to anyone who wants to learn some awesome math. His grading is very fair; it's just that his problems and homeworks are challenging and take a fair amount of time and effort to complete.

review_text: Dr.Shapiro is clearly very knowledgeable and passionate about ecology and evolution. Beyond that, I have very minimal positives to say. Like most of the reviews state, he is extremely disorganized in lecture and does not explicitly state what information you're supposed to take away from his extensive tangents. His note slides are very minimal, and often his "examples" are just screenshots of random research articles about the topic he is attempting to lecture on. His homework (only 5 points each) is a complete waste of time. They are often 5-8 questions, however, they take forever to complete because they are very intricate, which is hard to comprehend when you learn nothing but how to sleep with your eyes open during lecture. Additionally, his homework problems do not nearly resemble exam questions (even though he states they do). But I would probably say that the worst part of his class is the exams. However, most MC questions are formatted to trick you, and his fill-in-the-blanks are ridiculously specific. He will ask you to recall specific examples or videos he mentioned in lecture for 5 seconds. For example, one of his exam questions asked us to recall what organism a bird was mimicking from a 7-second video we watched in lecture once. His short-answer questions are relatively straightforward, which I can appreciate, and often, you will get partial credit on them for writing practically anything down. Additionally, he offers minimal extra credit (4 points total), which ultimately does nothing to your grade. He does drop your lowest midterm, but when their all extremely low scores, it honestly makes no difference. Overall, I quite literally would recommend taking any other professor. This class's material is not hard in the slightest, but his class is designed in a way that makes getting an A 10x harder than it should be. PS: For context, I have taken BSCI170, CHEM131, MATH135, and currently taking CHEM231, MATH136, alongside Dr. Shapiro's BSCI160 lecture, and his class will be the only reason my GPA will drop from a 4.0.

review_text: First off, Tianyi is definitely a nice guy. He tries his best to help students (making accommodations for taking exams in certain situations) and it's clear that he makes an effort to make the concepts come across to us while teaching. That being said, I think there's a lot that he can improve on. He is, no doubt, a very smart person, but there were a lot of times when he wasn't able to really teach certain topics effectively. Sometimes, it just felt like he was kinda reading off the slides not being truly engaged in the material. Secondly, the logistics of this class weren't the best. It took a month to get midterm grades back and all students were just left wondering what was going on. I would also mention that HWs and Piazza question took quite sometime to get responses to, but that's up to the TAs What swayed me to give a 3/5 is that at the end of the semester, he definitely listened to the concern of the students and implemented a couple of changes for the final exam to help us (allowing the use of a cheat sheet, a shorter exam overall because midterm was too long, etc). He also released practice/old exams for both the midterm and final exams ALONG WITH SOLUTIONS which is something CS profs don't always do and I really appreciated. Overall, I think you can succeed in this class if you just go to OH early and attend lecture.

review_text: Dr. Kim and Dr. Regli were co-teaching this semester (Fall 2025), so their lectures, homework, projects, and exams were the same. I think you should probably have some basic background in AI because I didn't, so that made all the concepts really hard to understand/follow. But this is a skill issue lol Some notes: - 3 coding projects. ACTUALLY DO PROJECT 1 WELL BEFORE THE DUE DATE PLEASE 🙏🙏🙏 It is the hardest project out of all 3. Even if they haven't taught the concepts yet, just use Google and stuff to learn, JUST DO IT EARLY!!!! All projects are coding + writing. For example, for Project 1, you had to write a full report alongside the code. - 4 homeworks. - 2 midterms and 1 final (non-cumulative). You're allowed a cheatsheet (front and back) for all exams. All exams are multiple choice, so no partial credit. - All lectures are recorded. - All slides are posted. - Optional 1-2 hour recitations/discussions where TAs or the professors explain some of the concepts or how to start a project. In my opinion, midterms 1 and 2 were too close together (I think they were a little over a month apart), but maybe my perception of time was warped lol. In either case, the content needed for the final feels like a whole year's worth of content with how dense it is. So don't be fooled by the "non-cumulative"; the final will always be hard for a conceptually challenging class like this one. Dr. Regli is an okay guy. His hats are fun. I haven't spoken to him one-on-one or asked for help during office hours, but I think he lectures okay...? The way he explains things can sometimes be contradictory and not that well-explained. I think to really understand his lectures, you have to read the book (optional), research/learn on your own, and review a lot. Piazza is not the greatest place to get clear answers. Dr. Regli tends to get a bit annoyed when students ask the same question, which is fair since there is a search bar in Piazza, but sometimes his answers to questions can come off as a bit condescending. It is kind of funny when he types out "sigh" though...

review_text: I want to start by saying that Dr. Rankin really is very nice. It's clear that all of the decisions she makes regarding the class are in an attempt to help students succeed, and she is VERY knowledgeable/passionate about the subject she is teaching. That being said, everything about this class stressed me out from beginning to end. The homework for this class was interesting, and I learned a lot from it, but it rarely helped at all with what you would see in the exams later on. She would also give practice quizzes, which were helpful in the sense that you would see what her exam style would be like, but they still didn't really help all that much. The only way I can describe the actual exams is hell on Earth. If Lucifer himself were to wake up one day and say, "Hey ^w^ I'm going to make an exam for these damned souls," they would look like the ones we took in this class. In fact, the whole class did so poorly on the first exam that she actually decided that she would let us retake it two days later, without changing the questions at all, because the average was like 40-50%. I learned after the first time that the only way to do well on the exams in this class is to take notes on every last slide in the presentations (50-80 slides each + many of the slides are just walls of text in size 12 font) and memorize, memorize, memorize as much as you can and then pray. I took BSCI170 last semester without having taken a biology or chemistry class since my freshman/sophomore year of high school, and I barely struggled at all in that class compared to what I have dealt with in this class thus far. I feel bad saying all of this because again, Dr. Rankin is so nice and so incredibly intelligent, but I have yet to meet anyone in my class of 100+ people that have said her teaching style works for them. It feels like 30 years have been taken off my life.
